section.title: Null Spaces, Column Spaces, Row Spaces, and Linear Transformations

content.heading: 4.2 Null Spaces, Column Spaces, Row Spaces, and Linear Transformations
content.paragraph: In applications of linear algebra, subspaces of $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ usually arise in one of two ways: (1) as the set of all solutions to a system of homogeneous linear equations or (2) as the set of all linear combinations of certain specified vectors. In this section, we compare and contrast these two descriptions of subspaces, allowing us to practice using the concept of a subspace. Actually, as you will soon discover, we have been working with subspaces ever since Section 1.3. The main new feature here is the terminology. The section concludes with a discussion of the kernel and range of a linear transformation.

Recall that the set of all $\textbf{x}$ that satisfy (1) is called the solution set of the system (1). Often it is convenient to relate this set directly to the matrix $A$ and the equation $A\mathbf{x} = 0$. We call the set of $\textbf{x}$ that satisfy $A\mathbf{x} = 0$ the null space of the matrix $A$.

note.title: Theorem 2
note.heading: Theorem 2
note.paragraph: The null space of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ is a subspace of $\text{ℝ}^{n}$. Equivalently, the set of all solutions to a system $A\textbf{x} = 0$ of $m$ homogeneous linear equations in $n$ unknowns is a subspace of $\text{ℝ}^{n}$.

content.heading: An Explicit Description of Nul A
content.paragraph: There is no obvious relation between vectors in Null $A$ and the entries in $A$. We say that Nul $A$ is defined implicitly, because it is defined by a condition that must be checked. No explicit list or description of the elements in Nul $A$ is given. However, solving the equation $A\textbf{x} = 0$ amounts to producing an explicit description of Nul $A$. The next example reviews the procedure from Section 1.5.

content.paragraph: Two points should be made about the solution of Example 3 that apply to all problems of this type where Nul $A$ contains nonzero vectors. We will use these facts later.

When Nul A contains nonzero vectors, the number of vectors in the spanning set for Nul A equals the number of free variables in the equation Ax=0.

content.heading: The Column Space of a Matrix
content.paragraph: Another important subspace associated with a matrix is its column space. Unlike the null space, the column space is defined explicitly via linear combinations.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition

content.paragraph: Since $\text{Span~}\left\{ \mathbf{a}_{1}\text{,}\text{…}\text{,}\mathbf{a}_{n} \right\}$ is a subspace, by Theorem 1, the next theorem follows from the definition of Col $A$ and the fact that the columns of $A$ are in $\text{ℝ}^{m}$.

note.title: Theorem 3
note.heading: Theorem 3
note.paragraph: The column space of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ is a subspace of $\text{ℝ}^{m}$.

content.paragraph: Note that a typical vector in Col $A$ can be written as $A\mathbf{x}$ for some $\textbf{x}$ because the notation $A\textbf{x}$ stands for a linear combination of the columns of $A$. That is,

The notation $A\textbf{x}$ for vectors in Col $A$ also shows that Col $A$ is the range of the linear transformation $\left. \textbf{x}\mapsto A\textbf{x} \right.$. We will return to this point of view at the end of the section.

content.paragraph: Recall from Theorem 4 in Section 1.4 that the columns of $A$ span $\text{ℝ}^{m}$ if and only if the equation $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$ has a solution for each $\textbf{b}$. We can restate this fact as follows:

note.paragraph: The column space of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ is all of $\text{ℝ}^{m}$ if and only if the equation $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$ has a solution for each $\textbf{b}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{m}$.

content.heading: The Row Space
content.paragraph: If $A$ is an $m \times n$ matrix, each row of $A$ has $n$ entries and thus can be identified with a vector in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$. The set of all linear combinations of the row vectors is called the row space of $A$ and is denoted by Row $A$. Each row has $n$ entries, so Row $A$ is a subspace of ${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$. Since the rows of $A$ are identified with the columns of $A^{T}$, we could also write $\text{Col~}A^{T}$ in place of Row $A$.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Let

The row space of $A$ is the subspace of $\text{ℝ}^{5}$ spanned by $\left\{ \mathbf{r}_{1},\mathbf{r}_{2},\mathbf{r}_{3},\mathbf{r}_{4} \right\}$. That is, Row$A = \text{Span}\ \left\{ \mathbf{r}_{1},\mathbf{r}_{2},\mathbf{r}_{3},\mathbf{r}_{4} \right\}$. It is natural to write row vectors horizontally; however, they may also be written as column vectors if that is more convenient.

content.heading: The Contrast Between Nul A and Col A
content.paragraph: It is natural to wonder how the null space and column space of a matrix are related. In fact, the two spaces are quite dissimilar, as Examples 6–8 will show. Nevertheless, a surprising connection between the null space and column space will emerge in Section 4.5, after more theory is available.

example.heading: Solution

content.paragraph: When a matrix is not square, as in Example 6, the vectors in Nul $A$ and Col $A$ live in entirely different “universes.” For example, no linear combination of vectors in $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ can produce a vector in $\text{ℝ}^{4}$. When $A$ is square, Nul $A$ and Col $A$ do have the zero vector in common, and in special cases it is possible that some nonzero vectors belong to both Nul $A$ and Col $A$.

content.heading: Kernel and Range of a Linear Transformation
content.paragraph: Subspaces of vector spaces other than $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ are often described in terms of a linear transformation instead of a matrix. To make this precise, we generalize the definition given in Section 1.8.

figure.caption: Contrast Between Nul A and Col A for an m×n Matrix A

image.alt: A table shows the difference between Nul A and Col A.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: A linear transformation T from a vector space $V$ into a vector space $W$ is a rule that assigns to each vector $\textbf{x}$ in $V$ a unique vector $T\left( \textbf{x} \right)$ in $W$, such that

list.item: (i)﻿T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v) for all u, v in V, and﻿
(ii)﻿T(cu)=cT(u) for all u in V and all scalars c.﻿

content.paragraph: The kernel or null space) of such a $T$ is the set of all $\mathbf{u}$ in $V$ such that $T(\mathbf{u}) = 0$ (the zero vector in $W$). The range of $T$ is the set of all vectors in $W$ of the form $T\left( \textbf{x} \right)$ for some $\mathbf{x}$ in $V$. If $T$ happens to arise as a matrix transformation—say, $T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$ for some matrix $A$—then the kernel and the range of $T$ are just the null space and the column space of $A$, as defined earlier.

It is not difficult to show that the kernel of $T$ is a subspace of $V$. The proof is essentially the same as the one for Theorem 2. Also, the range of $T$ is a subspace of $W$. See Figure 2 and Exercise 42.

figure.label: Figure 2
figure.caption: Subspaces associated with a linear transformation

image.alt: A figure shows two planes labeled V and W facing each other.

content.paragraph: In applications, a subspace usually arises as either the kernel or the range of an appropriate linear transformation. For instance, the set of all solutions of a homogeneous linear differential equation turns out to be the kernel of a linear transformation. Typically, such a linear transformation is described in terms of one or more derivatives of a function. To explain this in any detail would take us too far afield at this point. So we consider only two examples. The first explains why the operation of differentiation is a linear transformation.

example.heading: Example 9
(Calculus required)

Let $W$ be the vector space $C\lbrack a\text{,~}b\rbrack$ of all continuous functions on $\lbrack a\text{,~}b\rbrack$, and let $\left. D:V\rightarrow W \right.$ be the transformation that changes $f$ in $V$ into its derivative $f^{\prime}$. In calculus, two simple differentiation rules are

content.paragraph: A common technique used in the stock market is technical analysis. Statistical trends gathered from stock-trading activity, such as price movement and volume, are analyzed. Technical analysts focus on patterns of stock-price movements, trading signals, and various other analytical charting tools to evaluate a security’s strength or weakness. A moving average is a commonly used indicator in technical analysis. It smooths out price action by filtering out the effects from random price fluctuations. In the final example for this section, we examine the linear transformation that creates the two-day moving average from a “signal” of daily prices. We will look at moving average transformations that average over a longer period of time in Section 4.7.

example.heading: Example 11
example.paragraph: Let $\{ p_{k}\}$ in $\text{S}$ represent the price of a stock that has been recorded daily over an extended period of time. Note that we can assume that $p_{k} = 0$ for $k$ outside the time period under study. To create a two-day moving average, the mapping $\left. M_{2}:\mathbb{S}\rightarrow\mathbb{S} \right.$ defined by $M_{2}\left( \left\{ p_{k} \right\} \right) = \,\,\left\{ \frac{p_{k} + p_{k - 1}}{2} \right\}$ is applied to the data. Show that $M_{2}$ is a linear transformation and find its kernel.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: To see that $M_{2}$ is a linear transformation, observe that for two signals $\{ p_{k}\}$ and $\{ q_{k}\}$ in $\text{S}$ and any scalar $c$,
and

paragraph.math: $$M_{2}\mspace{-4mu}\left( c\left\{ p_{k} \right\} \right) = M_{2}\mspace{-4mu}\,{\mspace{-4mu}\left( \left\{ cp_{k} \right\} \right)} = \,\left\{ \frac{cp_{k} + cp_{k - 1}}{2} \right\}\, = c\left\{ \frac{p_{k} + p_{k - 1}}{2} \right\}\, = cM_{2}\mspace{-4mu}\,{\mspace{-4mu}\left( \left\{ p_{k} \right\} \right)}$$

example.paragraph: thus $M_{2}$ is a linear transformation.

To find the kernel of $M_{2}$, notice that $\left\{ p_{k} \right\}$ is in the kernel if and only if $\frac{p_{k} + p_{k - 1}}{2} = 0$ for all $k$, and hence $p_{k} = - p_{k - 1}$. Since this relationship is true for all integers $k$, it can be applied recursively resulting in $p_{k} = - p_{k - 1} = \left( {- 1} \right)^{2}p_{k - 2} = \left( {- 1} \right)^{3}p_{k - 3}\ldots$. Working out from $k = 0$, any signal in the kernel can be written as $p_{k} = p_{0}\left( {- 1} \right)^{k}$, a multiple of the alternating signal described by $\left\{ \left( {- 1} \right)^{k} \right\}$. Since the kernel of the two-day moving average function consists of all multiples of the alternating sequence, it smooths out daily fluctuations, without leveling out overall trends. (See Figure 3.)
